title: Lights on the control panel
ask: Should the new control panel have its own lights showing what is on (defog, recirc, mode, each seat's heat or cool level), or should the cluster screen show them?
why: The new panel has nine keys and four knobs, and nothing on it lights up to show what is on. The seat knobs have no end stops: they turn forever and count clicks, so once you let go, nothing on the panel tells you whether the seat is on heat 2 or cool 1. The same goes for the defogger, recirculate and the HVAC mode. The factory panel had a lamp for the defogger. Your answer decides whether the panel gets its own lights. If it does, the ribbon to the DCU grows from 20 to 26 wires, a small LED driver goes on the panel, and the faceplate needs windows for the lights. If it doesn't, the ICU's screen shows the state instead.
options:
(a) Lights on the panel: an LED by each key and a short row of LEDs for each knob's level, run by a small LED chip on the panel over the DCU's existing I2C bus. The ribbon goes from 20-way to 26-way (+2 data wires, +5 V and spares). About $5-10 more in parts. The faceplate has to leave room for the lights.
(b) No lights on the panel: the ICU screen shows the climate, seat and defog state, as a strip on every page or a pop-up when a knob moves. No parts, and the ribbon stays 20-way. You have to look at the cluster to see a setting.
(c) One light only, for the defogger, as the factory had. This still needs one more conductor, so the ribbon goes to 26-way. The seat levels are shown on the ICU screen as in (b).
recommend: (a), unless you want the dash kept dark and are happy glancing at the cluster to see a setting
stops: The ribbon's size (P157), the panel board's layout (H-008) and the faceplate's drawing

title: What the control panel is built on
ask: Should the control panel's switches, knobs and diodes sit on a small ordered circuit board, or be hand-wired?
why: The panel has no computer, but its 9 key switches, 9 diodes, 4 knobs, the mirror stick and the ribbon socket still have to be mounted and wired together behind the faceplate. The wiring itself is settled (D-380, D-452). This decides what it is built on. A circuit board gets ordered alongside the DCU board, and the knobs and switches solder straight onto it. Hand wiring is free, but it means about 40 point-to-point wires behind the dash.
options:
(a) A small circuit board, ordered in the same order as the DCU board: about $10-20 more. The knobs and switches line up exactly with the faceplate, and it holds the lights if the panel gets its own lights. The faceplate has to be drawn first so that the board's holes match it.
(b) Hand-wired on perfboard or point-to-point: no extra cost, but more hours at the bench. The diodes become leaded parts instead of the tiny surface-mount ones. It is harder to line the knobs up with the faceplate holes, and harder to service.
recommend: (a), unless you would rather spend bench hours than about $15
stops: The panel's layout (H-008) and its parts list (P155)
